Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Data Governance and Access Control
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Data Governance and Access Control

Design role hierarchies, assign privileges with SQL, manage ownership, and automate permissions with future grants so your Snowflake environment is secure and simple to administer.

In this lesson

Understand RBAC principles, create custom roles, grant privileges, transfer ownership, and configure future grants to reduce admin work.

Why it matters

Proper governance prevents data leaks, ensures compliance, and enables teams to do their jobs without risky over-privilege.

Concept map
Roles
Grant privileges to roles; assign roles to users.
Ownership
Owner role has full control; transfer preserves grants with a clause.
Future grants
Apply privileges automatically to future objects in a container.
Auditing
Use SHOW GRANTS to review role privileges and history.
RBAC Principles

Roles hold privileges; users receive roles.

Ownership

Creator role becomes owner by default.

Future Grants

New objects inherit grants automatically.

Explore Key Topics
Create and grant roles
Use CREATE ROLE and GRANT ROLE TO ROLE to build inheritance.
Ownership & transfer
Transfer ownership with COPY CURRENT GRANTS to preserve existing permissions.
Future grants
Apply SELECT on future tables to a role so new tables are accessible immediately.

screens.title: RBAC Fundamentals in Snowflake
screens.narratorSegment: Role-Based Access Control puts permissions on roles and then assigns those roles to users. In Snowflake, a role is an entity you can grant privileges to and also grant to other roles. This design lets administrators define a permission once and reuse it across users and teams. For example, you might grant SELECT on a sales schema to a DATA_ANALYST role and then give that role to every analyst. That way, adding a new analyst is a single GRANT ROLE operation instead of many individual privilege grants. A common misconception is that roles are simply labels for users. In practice they are permission containers that can be composed. Another misconception is that privileges granted to one role are private; when you grant a role to another role, privileges flow by inheritance and become part of the recipient's effective set. A concrete example from this chapter: create DATA_ANALYST and grant USAGE on a warehouse and SELECT on tables. Then grant DATA_ANALYST to DATA_ENGINEER so engineers inherit analyst read access in addition to their own create-table rights. The takeaway: think in terms of permission buckets you can reuse and compose. How would you model read-only and dev access for a small team?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A role is a permission container that can be granted privileges and granted to users or other roles to create inheritance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › RBAC Fundamentals
Definition

Role as a permission container

A role holds privileges and can be assigned to users or other roles. Design roles to match responsibilities, not individuals.

Concrete example
Create DATA_ANALYST, grant SELECT on SALES_DB, then grant that role to users who need read access.
Common misconception
Roles are not just labels. They carry privileges and can be composed into hierarchies to inherit permissions.
Key takeaway
Model permissions as reusable buckets to simplify onboarding and auditing.
Illustration
Scenario: analyst access
-- As SECURITYADMIN
CREATE ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE COMPUTE_WH TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE SALES_DB TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA SALES_DB.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA SALES_DB.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
This series of grants gives analysts the ability to run queries without granting write or ownership privileges.
Check your understanding
If you grant DATA_ANALYST to DATA_ENGINEER, what privileges does an engineer have? Think about inherited read access and their own extra rights.

screens.title: System-Defined Roles vs Custom Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake ships with system-defined roles that serve specific administrative purposes. ACCOUNTADMIN holds the broadest privileges and should be used sparingly. SYSADMIN is intended for database and warehouse operations, SECURITYADMIN manages users and role grants, USERADMIN manages user creation and role assignment, and PUBLIC is a default role automatically assigned to all users. These roles are useful for account-level tasks and for delegating specialized administration. However, most day-to-day access should be handled by custom roles tailored to business functions. Custom roles let you match privileges to team responsibilities—DATA_ANALYST, DATA_ENGINEER, FINANCE_READER, and so on. A useful comparison is to treat system roles like platform-level operators and custom roles like team-level permission sets. A common mistake is using ACCOUNTADMIN for routine work; this grants excessive power and increases risk. Another pitfall is assigning privileges to PUBLIC unintentionally, which exposes resources broadly. Example: create FINANCE_READER with SELECT on a finance schema rather than granting SELECT to PUBLIC. The takeaway: use system roles for platform administration and custom roles to express business access patterns. System-Defined Roles vs Custom Roles means system roles are for platform operations; custom roles map to business functions and reduce risk when used correctly.. In practical terms, when to rely on built-in roles and when to create custom roles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › System-Defined Roles vs Custom Roles
System-Defined Roles
ACCOUNTADMIN
Full account control; use sparingly and only for platform-level tasks.
SYSADMIN
Manage warehouses, databases, and create objects.
SECURITYADMIN
Manage users, roles, and grants.
USERADMIN
Create and manage users and assign roles.
PUBLIC
Automatically assigned; avoid granting sensitive privileges here.
Warning
Do not use ACCOUNTADMIN for daily tasks. Overuse increases security risk and audit scope.
Custom Roles
Purpose
Model business functions and group privileges by job responsibility.
Hierarchy
Grant roles to roles to create inheritance and reduce repetition.
Example
Create DATA_ANALYST with SELECT and grant it to DATA_ENGINEER to inherit read access.
Best practice
Use custom roles for daily operations; reserve system roles for administration.

screens.title: Create Roles and Grant Privileges
screens.narratorSegment: Creating roles and assigning privileges follows a repeatable process. First, create the role using CREATE ROLE. Second, grant the role the necessary USAGE and object privileges such as SELECT or CREATE TABLE depending on the role's responsibilities. Third, create role relationships by granting a role to another role when you want inheritance. Fourth, assign roles to users with GRANT ROLE TO USER. A concrete example from the chapter shows creating DATA_ANALYST and DATA_ENGINEER, granting usage on a warehouse and SELECT on tables to DATA_ANALYST, then granting DATA_ANALYST to DATA_ENGINEER so engineers inherit read privileges and retain additional create rights. A common pitfall is forgetting to grant USAGE on the database and schema; without USAGE the SELECT privilege on tables is ineffective. Another misconception is that granting a role to a user automatically grants the user access to warehouses; you must explicitly grant USAGE on warehouses. Practice: after creating roles and grants, verify with SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE and SHOW GRANTS TO USER to confirm expected privileges. Which grants would you run first for a new read-only role? Create Roles and Grant Privileges means create role, grant necessary usage and object privileges, compose hierarchies, then assign to users and audit.. In practical terms, step-by-step sql patterns to define roles and assign object privileges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stepwise grants
keyIdea.text: Create role, grant necessary USAGE and object privileges, compose hierarchies, then assign to users and audit.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Create Roles & Grant Privileges
Process
  1. Create the role as SECURITYADMIN or a role with CREATE ROLE privilege.
  2. Grant USAGE on warehouses, databases, and schemas as required.
  3. Grant object privileges like SELECT or CREATE TABLE to the role.
  4. Grant roles to other roles to form a hierarchy if needed.
  5. Grant roles to users and verify with SHOW GRANTS.
Pitfall: Without USAGE on database and schema, table-level privileges won't let users query data.
Example SQL
-- As SECURITYADMIN or equivalent
CREATE ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
CREATE ROLE DATA_ENGINEER;

-- Inherit analyst privileges in engineer role
GRANT ROLE DATA_ANALYST TO ROLE DATA_ENGINEER;

-- Grants for DATA_ANALYST
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE COMPUTE_WH TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE SALES_DB TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA SALES_DB.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA SALES_DB.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;

-- Additional engineer privileges
GRANT CREATE TABLE ON SCHEMA SALES_DB.RAW_DATA TO ROLE DATA_ENGINEER;
Run verification queries like SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST to confirm the assigned rights.

screens.title: Granting Roles to Users and Switching Context
screens.narratorSegment: Once roles exist, administer them to users and use role context to operate with specific privileges. As SECURITYADMIN or a similarly privileged role, grant roles to users with GRANT ROLE TO USER. In the chapter example, DATA_ANALYST is granted to JOHN_DOE and DATA_ENGINEER to JANE_SMITH. Users can have multiple roles. At runtime they choose a role to adopt using the USE ROLE command. Their effective privileges are the union of the role they select and any roles granted to that role through hierarchy. A typical confusion is thinking a user holds all privileges they have ever been granted automatically; privileges apply according to the active role context. Another subtle point: default_role for a user determines what role is active on login, but users can change roles during a session. Example: a developer might have DATA_ENGINEER as default to create objects, then switch to DATA_ANALYST to run read-only queries for verification. Practice: after granting a role, ask the user to USE ROLE and run a SELECT to confirm access, and then try CREATE TABLE to see if write rights are absent or present based on role.

keyIdea.text: Grant roles to users and remember that active role context controls effective permissions during a session.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Grant Roles & Switch Context
Granting
Use GRANT ROLE to assign roles to users. Set DEFAULT_ROLE on user creation to define the initial session role.
-- As SECURITYADMIN
GRANT ROLE DATA_ANALYST TO USER JOHN_DOE;
GRANT ROLE DATA_ENGINEER TO USER JANE_SMITH;

-- Create user with default role
CREATE USER ANNA_SMITH PASSWORD = 'password123' DEFAULT_ROLE = FINANCE_DEV;
GRANT ROLE FINANCE_DEV TO USER ANNA_SMITH;
Verification: have the user USE ROLE and run a SELECT to confirm read rights, then try a write to check for missing privileges.
Runtime behavior
A user's active role determines the privileges available. Switching roles changes effective permissions immediately for that session.
Concrete scenario
An engineer sets DATA_ENGINEER as default to create tables, then switches to DATA_ANALYST to run read-only reports, preventing accidental writes.

screens.title: Ownership and Transferring Ownership
screens.narratorSegment: OWNERSHIP in Snowflake is a special privilege that confers full control of an object to the owning role. When an object is created, the active role becomes its owner. Ownership allows the owner to grant or revoke all privileges, drop the object, and transfer ownership. Transferring ownership requires care because it can remove privileges unless you include the COPY CURRENT GRANTS clause. This clause preserves existing grants so access continuity is maintained. A common misconception is treating OWNERSHIP as just another privilege that any admin can set freely; ownership changes are restricted and must be performed by the current owner or a role with MANAGE GRANTS. A concrete example: if a team is reorganized and a new role should own a table, use GRANT OWNERSHIP ON TABLE TO ROLE COPY CURRENT GRANTS so users keep their existing permissions. The takeaway: use ownership transfer sparingly and always consider the COPY CURRENT GRANTS option to avoid accidental permission loss. Ownership and Transferring Ownership means ownership gives full control; transfer ownership using copy current grants to preserve existing grants and avoid breaking access.. In practical terms, how ownership differs and how to change an object's owner safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ownership rules
keyIdea.text: Ownership gives full control; transfer ownership using COPY CURRENT GRANTS to preserve existing grants and avoid breaking access.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Ownership & Transfer
What is ownership?

Ownership grants the owning role complete control over an object. The creator role becomes the owner by default.

-- Transfer ownership while preserving grants
GRANT OWNERSHIP ON TABLE SALES_DB.PUBLIC.ORDERS TO ROLE NEW_OWNER COPY CURRENT GRANTS;
Note: COPY CURRENT GRANTS preserves existing privileges so users retain access after transfer.
Common pitfalls
  • Changing ownership without COPY CURRENT GRANTS can revoke existing privileges.
  • Assuming any admin can transfer ownership; only the owner or MANAGE GRANTS can do so.
  • Not auditing ownership changes increases risk of orphaned or inaccessible objects.
Takeaway
Plan ownership transfers and include COPY CURRENT GRANTS to maintain continuity.

screens.title: Future Grants: Automating Permissions
screens.narratorSegment: Future grants let you apply privileges to objects that do not yet exist inside a container such as a database or schema. Instead of manually granting SELECT each time a new table appears, configure GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA... TO ROLE. This ensures that any future table will automatically have the specified privilege for that role. Use future grants for tables and views when teams generate new objects regularly. A common mistake is to assume future grants also affect objects created in different schemas or databases; they apply only within the specified container. Another pitfall is granting both ALL and FUTURE grants redundantly; plan your grant strategy to avoid confusion. Example commands include granting SELECT on future tables and views in SALES_DB. PUBLIC to DATA_ANALYST. After applying future grants, verify with SHOW FUTURE GRANTS to confirm the configuration. The takeaway: future grants scale permissions reliably and reduce the chance of missing access for new objects, but they must be scoped carefully to the intended container. Pattern
Use GRANT ... ON FUTURE TABLES or FUTURE VIEWS to assign privileges that apply to future objects in the specified schema or database.
-- As SECURITYADMIN
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA SALES_DB.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE VIEWS IN SCHEMA SALES_DB.PUBLIC TO ROLE DATA_ANALYST;
Verify future grants with SHOW FUTURE GRANTS and be careful to scope by schema or database.
Concrete benefit
When tables are created by pipelines or users, future grants ensure access is available immediately without manual updates.
Example scenario
A nightly ETL creates new partitioned tables. With future grants in place, analysts retain SELECT access for those tables automatically.
Misconception: future grants do not retroactively modify existing objects. Use ALL TABLES or explicit grants for current objects and FUTURE grants for new ones.

screens.title: Auditing Grants and Common Mistakes

SHOW FUTURE GRANTS helps you verify automated permissions for objects created later. Regular audits reveal stale roles, excessive privileges, or grants assigned to PUBLIC by accident. A frequent mistake is granting ACCOUNTADMIN or other high-power system roles for convenience; this expands attack surface and complicates compliance. Another common error is granting privileges directly to users instead of to roles, which makes later changes time-consuming. In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of Role-Based Access Control in Snowflake and why it matters for secure, scalable data platforms. You will learn what a role is, how system-defined roles differ from custom roles, and how a role hierarchy simplifies permission management. We will also walk through the practical S Q L used to create roles, grant privileges, assign roles to users, transfer ownership, and configure future grants so new tables inherit the right access automatically. These capabilities reduce manual work and lower the chance of over-privileging users. As you follow the visual topics, notice how an administrator can grant a privilege once to a role and then assign that role to many users, instead of repeating grant statements per user. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a small role hierarchy for a team, apply future grants for new objects, and avoid common mistakes such as giving account-level power to daily operators. Think about a real dataset you manage and how a clear role structure could limit access without slowing work.

In this section we set clear, measurable objectives so you know what competence looks like. You will be able to explain Role-Based Access Control as a model where permissions are assigned to roles rather than to each user. You will learn to identify Snowflake's system-defined roles and when to rely on them versus creating custom roles for your teams. You will also practice designing a hierarchical role structure that mirrors business responsibilities, so privileges can be inherited rather than repeatedly granted. Finally, you will be introduced to S Q L commands for granting and revoking privileges and to the future grants feature which automatically applies permissions to objects created later. Each objective connects a specific skill to a practical outcome: fewer manual grants, clearer audits, and safer daily operations. Consider a scenario where a new analyst needs read-only access to sales data; these objectives will guide you to create a role, assign the necessary grants, and use future grants to keep access consistent when new tables appear.

These applied objectives focus on hands-on skills and operational checks you will use in a Snowflake account. First, you will implement a hierarchical role structure that matches team responsibilities, granting lower-level roles to higher-level roles so privileges flow upward. Second, you will learn to grant and revoke privileges on warehouses, databases, schemas, tables and views using the S Q L patterns shown. Third, you will use future grants to automatically assign privileges to tables and views created later, saving administrative effort. Fourth, you will perform audits of role grants and future grants using the appropriate SHOW commands to verify that permissions match policy. Each skill links to a practical outcome: a new hire can perform required queries without unnecessary access, administrators can onboard new objects safely, and auditors can confirm compliance. Takeaway: the value of RBAC is not only in simpler commands but in predictable, auditable access behavior across time.

Role-Based Access Control puts permissions on roles and then assigns those roles to users. In Snowflake, a role is an entity you can grant privileges to and also grant to other roles. This design lets administrators define a permission once and reuse it across users and teams. For example, you might grant SELECT on a sales schema to a DATA_ANALYST role and then give that role to every analyst. That way, adding a new analyst is a single GRANT ROLE operation instead of many individual privilege grants. A common misconception is that roles are simply labels for users. In practice they are permission containers that can be composed. Another misconception is that privileges granted to one role are private; when you grant a role to another role, privileges flow by inheritance and become part of the recipient's effective set. A concrete example from this chapter: create DATA_ANALYST and grant USAGE on a warehouse and SELECT on tables. Then grant DATA_ANALYST to DATA_ENGINEER so engineers inherit analyst read access in addition to their own create-table rights. The takeaway: think in terms of permission buckets you can reuse and compose. How would you model read-only and dev access for a small team?

Snowflake ships with system-defined roles that serve specific administrative purposes. ACCOUNTADMIN holds the broadest privileges and should be used sparingly. SYSADMIN is intended for database and warehouse operations, SECURITYADMIN manages users and role grants, USERADMIN manages user creation and role assignment, and PUBLIC is a default role automatically assigned to all users. These roles are useful for account-level tasks and for delegating specialized administration. However, most day-to-day access should be handled by custom roles tailored to business functions. Custom roles let you match privileges to team responsibilities—DATA_ANALYST, DATA_ENGINEER, FINANCE_READER, and so on. A useful comparison is to treat system roles like platform-level operators and custom roles like team-level permission sets. A common mistake is using ACCOUNTADMIN for routine work; this grants excessive power and increases risk. Another pitfall is assigning privileges to PUBLIC unintentionally, which exposes resources broadly. Example: create FINANCE_READER with SELECT on a finance schema rather than granting SELECT to PUBLIC. The takeaway: use system roles for platform administration and custom roles to express business access patterns. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating roles and assigning privileges follows a repeatable process. First, create the role using CREATE ROLE. Second, grant the role the necessary USAGE and object privileges such as SELECT or CREATE TABLE depending on the role's responsibilities. Third, create role relationships by granting a role to another role when you want inheritance. Fourth, assign roles to users with GRANT ROLE TO USER.
